sourceLabel: Final Exam — practice (computer part), simple case
intro: The Final's graph programming section asks you to extend Graph<T> with a new traversal method on top of your Milestone 1 work. Practice that exact pattern by adding a public int numDirectedTriangles() method to your Graph<T> (or its AL/AM subclasses) that returns the number of directed 3-cycles in the graph — that is, ordered triples of distinct vertices (u, v, w) with edges u→v, v→w, w→u. Then paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java for a self-check. The simple 3-vertex case is the warm-up; harder variants follow.
hints: A directed triangle (u, v, w) requires three directed edges: u→v, v→w, and w→u. The simplest correct implementation iterates over all ordered triples of distinct vertices and checks the three edges via hasEdge — but it must not double-count.

The triple (A, B, C) and (B, C, A) and (C, A, B) describe the same triangle (a 3-cycle has three rotations). One way to count each triangle exactly once is to enforce a fixed ordering on the triple — e.g. require u to compare-less-than both v and w using vertex.toString().

If you're seeing 6 where the test expects 2, you're counting each triangle three times (once per rotation). Either divide by 3 at the end, or restrict to one canonical rotation per triangle as described above.

sourceLabel: Final Exam — practice (computer part), example graph
intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method as the warm-up, now on a 6-vertex example from the Final practice's computer part. The graph below has exactly 3 directed triangles after all 9 edges are added. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the simple case passes. If your count is wildly off, the bug is usually rotation-double-counting; if it's off by one or two, you may be misreading the edge list — sketch the adjacency list on paper first.
hints: Build the adjacency list on paper before running. From A: A→B. From B: B→C, B→D. From C: C→A, C→E, C→F. From D: D→E. From E: E→B, E→F. From F: nothing. With those edges in hand, scan for closed 3-cycles by inspection — that gives you the answer to compare against your code.

If you're seeing 9 instead of 3, you're counting each of the three triangles three times (one per rotation). If you're seeing 6 or 18, you're counting both rotations AND reflections — but in a directed graph there is no reflection symmetry, so check your loop bounds.

A reliable iteration shape: for u in keySet(), for v in successorSet(u), for w in successorSet(v) — if hasEdge(w, u) and {u,v,w} are pairwise distinct, increment. Then divide the running count by 3 once at the end.

sourceLabel: Final Exam — practice (computer part), large graph perf
intro: Same numDirectedTriangles() method, now graded for performance on a 150-vertex complete graph (every ordered pair of distinct vertices has an edge in each direction). The closed-form count is N(N-1)(N-2) ordered triples; how that divides depends on whether your implementation counts each triangle once, three times, or six times — match the divisor you used in the earlier drills. The test asserts both correctness and a 1-second wall-clock budget. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone1ALTest.java after the example case passes. Perf hints below.
hints: successorIterator construction must be O(1). If you're calling successorSet (which eagerly builds a HashSet) inside an inner loop, you're allocating O(N) sets per outer step — that's an N^4 algorithm. Use successorIterator directly or cache successorSet outside the loop.

hasEdge in AdjacencyListGraph walks the successors list of `from` looking for `to`. For a complete graph that's an O(N) call. Inside a triple-nested vertex loop, that becomes O(N^4). For this drill, prefer the (u → v → w → u?) shape over (u, v, w from keySet, hasEdge three times) — it visits only real edges, not all triples.

If you're timing out at exactly 1 second, profile by halving size and confirming wall time drops by ~8× (cubic scaling) and not ~16× (quartic). If it drops by 16×, your inner loop has a hidden O(N) step you can hoist out.

intro: The Final's graph programming section often asks for a BFS-flavored method that's related to shortestPath but not identical — practice that pattern by implementing public int countReachableWithinKHops(T from, int k) on your Graph<T> (or in AdjacencyListGraph if you prefer): it returns the count of vertices reachable from `from` using at most k directed edges, including `from` itself at hop 0. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone2ALTest.java. Note: that file's existing @Test methods route through Core helpers and don't import assertEquals directly — add `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;` at the top before the test compiles.
hints: Standard BFS with explicit hop tracking: keep a Queue of (vertex, distance) pairs and a HashSet of visited vertices. Pop one at a time, skip if already visited, mark visited, count it. Push successors (via successorIterator) only when their distance is ≤ k.

Off-by-one trap: countReachableWithinKHops(start, 0) returns 1 — the start vertex itself counts at distance 0. countReachableWithinKHops(start, 1) returns 1 plus the number of distinct direct successors. The hop count is the number of edges traversed, not the number of vertices visited.

Don't call successorSet inside the BFS inner loop — it eagerly builds a HashSet per call. Use successorIterator for O(1) construction. Eager construction blows an O(V+E) BFS up to O(V·E) or worse, which is exactly what the Final's perf-bound version of this question is designed to catch.

intro: Your Milestone 2 stronglyConnectedComponent returns the SCC containing one specific key. The Final practice's graph section often asks for a related-but-different question: 'is the entire graph one big SCC?' Practice it by implementing public boolean isStronglyConnected() on your Graph<T> that returns true iff every vertex can reach every other vertex. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone2ALTest.java. As with the BFS drill, you'll need to add `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;` and `import java.util.HashSet;` at the top — neither is currently in M2ALTest's import block.
hints: Algorithm: pick any vertex v from keySet(). Do a forward BFS from v (via successorIterator) — collect every vertex it reaches. Do a reverse BFS from v (via predecessorIterator) — collect every vertex that reaches it. The graph is strongly connected iff both reachable sets equal keySet().

Why one vertex is sufficient: if v reaches everyone (forward) and everyone reaches v (reverse), then for any pair a, b, the path a → v → b exists (concatenate reverse-of-a-to-v with forward-of-v-to-b). You don't have to check V·V pairs separately.

Edge case: a single-vertex graph is trivially strongly connected — its lone vertex reaches itself with the zero-length path. Your BFS will visit only the start vertex, the reachable set is {v}, keySet() is {v}, and the comparison naturally returns true. If your code special-cases size 1 to false, you've added a bug.

intro: This is the Winter 2023 Final's graph problem, reproduced from the exam's own test cases. Implement public Set<T> findUnknownBalloons(Set<T> confirmedBalloons, Set<T> allBalloons) on your Graph<T>: it returns the set of balloons not in the same network (SCC) as any confirmed balloon. If your Milestone 2 stronglyConnectedComponent is working, this is a thin layer on top. The non-solution reference doc (linked above) describes the problem semantics with worked examples. Paste this warmup test into GraphSurfingMilestone2ALTest.java — you'll need four imports the existing test class doesn't have: `import java.util.HashSet;`, `import java.util.Set;`, `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;`, and `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue;`.
hints: Skeleton: for each balloon b in confirmedBalloons, compute its SCC via your Milestone 2 method, and accumulate those SCCs into a single HashSet of 'known' balloons. Then return allBalloons minus that known set.

Why {B} alone and {C} alone give the same answer: B and C form a 2-cycle (B → C → B), so stronglyConnectedComponent(B) and stronglyConnectedComponent(C) both return {B, C}. A and E never participate in any cycle, so their SCCs are singletons.

If your test fails on the third sub-case (confirmed = {A, E}, expected unknowns = {B, C}): make sure you're computing the SCC of each confirmed balloon, not just adding it to the known set. SCC({A}) = {A} alone because no edge reaches A from elsewhere; you must consult the graph to figure that out.

intro: Same findUnknownBalloons method, now on the 2023 Final's 9-vertex example with three distinct networks: {A,B,C,D} (a ring), {E,F} (a 2-cycle), {G,H} (a 2-cycle), and {I} (isolated). Confirming any balloon transitively confirms its whole network. Paste this test into GraphSurfingMilestone2ALTest.java after the warmup passes. Same four imports required (see warmup intro).
hints: The B → E edge does NOT put B and E in the same network. Networks are SCCs (mutual reachability), and E has no way to reach B. So confirming {A} confirms {A, B, C, D} only — E, F, G, H, I remain unknown.

Don't recompute the SCC for balloons you've already covered. If A and B are both confirmed, and you've already added stronglyConnectedComponent(A) = {A,B,C,D} to your known set, computing stronglyConnectedComponent(B) is redundant work that returns the same set. Skip B if it's already in known.

Edge case in the third sub-case: confirming {I} alone — I is a solo vertex with no edges, so SCC({I}) = {I}. The unknown set is everything else (8 balloons). Your code should handle this without crashing on the no-edges case.
